title: Bessara
subtitle: Moroccan dried fava bean soup
excerpt: A thick, creamy soup of dried fava beans pureed with olive oil, cumin, paprika, and garlic. A staple of Moroccan winter breakfasts and street food, drizzled with more olive oil and chilli before serving.
sourceNotes: Bessara (or bisara) is a dried fava bean soup eaten as breakfast street food throughout Morocco and parts of Algeria. Cross-referenced with Paula Wolfert, Couscous and Other Good Food from Morocco (1973) and Anissa Helou, Feast (2018).

recipe.freezeNotes: Freezes well for up to 3 months. Thickens further on freezing; add water when reheating.
recipe.batchNotes: Doubles well. The soup improves the next day.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Fava beans must soak for 8 hours or overnight. The soup keeps in the fridge for 3 days.

content.text: Bessara is a smooth, thick purée-soup made from split dried fava beans that have been soaked overnight and then simmered until very soft. The seasoning is cumin, paprika, and garlic; the finish is a generous drizzle of olive oil. It is a winter breakfast food in Morocco, sold from roadside stalls where it is ladled into bowls and eaten with bread.

items.prepNote: dried split fava beans, soaked overnight in cold water and drained

content.text: Put the drained fava beans in a large saucepan with the garlic cloves and enough cold water to cover by 5 cm. Bring to the boil and skim off any foam. Reduce heat and simmer for 45 to 60 minutes until the beans are very soft and beginning to fall apart.

Drain the beans, reserving the cooking liquid. Transfer to a blender with the cumin, paprika, olive oil, lemon juice, and salt. Blend until completely smooth, adding enough of the reserved cooking liquid to achieve the consistency of thick soup.
Taste and adjust: more cumin, more lemon, more salt as needed. The bessara should be thick enough to coat the back of a spoon.
Ladle into bowls. Drizzle generously with olive oil, dust with cumin and paprika, and add chilli flakes or a spoonful of harissa. Serve with warm flatbread.

items.cause: Too much cooking liquid added when blending
items.fix: Return to a saucepan and simmer uncovered to reduce. Or add less cooking liquid initially and add more to adjust.

items.symptom: The beans are still firm after 1 hour
items.cause: Old dried beans or not soaked long enough
items.fix: Old beans can take much longer. Continue cooking and check every 15 minutes. Always buy dried beans from a shop with good turnover.

items.cause: Not enough cumin or insufficient salt
items.fix: Add more cumin and a good squeeze of lemon. Taste before serving; the soup should be assertively seasoned.

items.cause: Not blended long enough or beans not soft enough
items.fix: Blend for longer, or strain through a fine sieve for a very smooth result.

content.text: Bessara is eaten from wooden or ceramic bowls alongside round flatbread (khobz) at market stalls across northern Morocco from Fez to Marrakech. It is winter food: filling, cheap, warming. The stall keeper portions it from a large terracotta pot, adds the olive oil, cumin, and harissa at the last moment. It is closely related to Egyptian bessara, which is made from dried broad beans or green peas and is green rather than ochre from the inclusion of herbs; the Moroccan version is plainer and more austere.
